title: BEE Showcases Commercial Electric Cooking Solutions to Accelerate India's Transition from LPG to Electricity
subtitle: Invites stakeholders to register for the Go Electric Commercial Electric Cooking Vendor Directory
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                10 SEP 2026 7:33PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE), Ministry of Power, Government of India, organized the “Commercial Induction Cooking Showcase & Chef Challenge” in New Delhi, under the theme “Accelerating India’s Electric Cooking Ambition: From Technology Demonstration to Real-World Adoption.” The event brought together policymakers, public sector enterprises, manufacturers, technology providers, chefs, hoteliers, and commercial kitchen operators on a common platform to advance the adoption of energy-efficient electric cooking in India’s commercial and institutional kitchens.
Shri Pankaj Agarwal, Secretary, Ministry of Power, was the Chief Guest. He inaugurated an exhibition featuring commercial e-cooking appliances and technologies from seven leading manufacturers. Shri Krushna Chandra Panigrahy, Director General, BEE, delivered the keynote address, and Ms. Neha Dhingra, Director, CLASP, delivered the welcome address.
Addressing the gathering, Shri Pankaj Agarwal noted that energy security is the real driver behind India's shift to electric cooking. Due to the ongoing global conflict and rising price of LPG, transitioning to e-cooking is not only a strategic shift but also an operational choice. He stated that the enabling base for this transition already exists, citing schemes such as Pradhan Mantri Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana (SAUBHAGYA) and PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana, which provide a strong foundation for promoting e-cooking appliances in the residential sector. At the same time, he acknowledged that the barriers to wider adoption have been behavioural and infrastructural, ranging from chef and consumer comfort with the taste of food cooked on induction to gaps in local distribution capacity. Looking ahead, he identified awareness creation as the fastest lever to drive demand and accelerate the mainstreaming of electric cooking across the country.
In his keynote address, Shri Krushna Chandra Panigrahy, Director General, BEE, welcomed representatives from the Ministry of Power, CLASP, industry, hospitality, PSUs, manufacturers, and chefs, and thanked them for their role in advancing India's e-cooking ecosystem. He said India's energy transition isn't just about cleaner energy sources; it is also about using energy more efficiently, and electric cooking brings together efficiency, energy security, convenience, and sustainability in one shift. He announced that BEE is inviting manufacturers, distributors, system integrators, and solution providers to register for the Go Electric Commercial Electric Cooking Vendor Directory, a public platform that will help hotels, restaurants, canteens, hospitals, and institutions find credible providers. He also shared that BEE is working with the Bureau of Indian Standards to develop a Standards & Labeling framework for commercial induction hobs. Shri. Panigrahy informed that BEE’s objective is to move beyond individual demonstration projects towards a mature commercial e-cooking ecosystem, "where users have confidence in the technology, manufacturers understand market requirements, and policymakers have the evidence needed to support its scale-up."
The inaugural session was followed by a Commercial Induction Chef Challenge, where three chefs prepared dishes using induction cooktops. The demonstration enabled participants to observe the cooking performance, ease of use, heat control, and cooking time of induction technology.
The event concluded with closing remarks from BEE, reiterating the Bureau’s commitment to working with the Ministry of Power, CLASP, manufacturers, industry associations, public sector enterprises and commercial kitchen operators to accelerate the adoption of energy-efficient electric cooking across India.
The event reaffirmed the shared responsibility of the Government, industry and hospitality sector to move India’s commercial kitchens from technology demonstration to real-world adoption, in line with the vision of a Viksit and Atmanirbhar Bharat.
About BEE
The Government of India set up the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) on1st March, 2002 under the provisions of the Energy Conservation Act, 2001. The mission of the Bureau of Energy Efficiency is to assist in developing policies and strategies with a thrust on self-regulation and market principles.
A key objective is reducing the energy intensity of the Indian economy. BEE coordinates with designated consumers, designated agencies and other organizations. It recognises, identifies and utilises the existing resources and infrastructure, in performing the functions assigned to it under the Act. The Act also provides for regulatory and promotional functions.

title: Union Minister Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan Launches Operational Guidelines for DILRMP 3.0
subtitle:
Central Sector Scheme approved with an outlay of ₹565.50 Crore for 2026–2031 to establish an integrated, GIS-based ‘Land Stack’

Sub-Registrar Offices to be upgraded into modern ‘Registration Seva Kendras’ modeled after Passport Seva Kendras

Every land parcel to receive a 14-digit Bhu-Aadhaar (ULPIN) alongside full georeferencing of cadastral maps

“Land is not merely property; it represents the pride of farmers and our generational heritage”: Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                10 SEP 2026 10:01PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister for Rural Development, Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan, formally launched the Operational Guidelines for the Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme (DILRMP) 3.0 during a hybrid event held at Krishi Bhawan today. The launch brought together State Revenue and Registration Ministers, Principal Secretaries, and senior officials from across the country via video conferencing.
Addressing the gathering, Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan stated that DILRMP 3.0 is a decisive step toward improving Ease of Living for rural citizens, farmers, and property owners. He underscored that land in India is deeply tied to emotional and familial identities, making accurate and accessible documentation vital.
“Land is not just a piece of soil; it is the pride of our farmers, the blessing of our ancestors, and the identity of future generations,”
said the Union Minister.
The Minister pointed out that the earlier phases of DILRMP successfully digitized 99.90% of Records of Rights (RoRs) and 97% of cadastral maps, alongside computerizing 99% of Sub-Registrar Offices (SROs). He noted that DILRMP 3.0 now raises the bar by moving from isolated digitization to full system integration, ensuring farmers can secure institutional credit easily and citizens are spared repeated visits to government offices.
Speaking on the occasion, Minister of State for Rural Development, Dr. Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani, highlighted that DILRMP 3.0 will resolve legacy challenges by focusing on spatial accuracy, georeferenced maps, and seamless interoperability across departments.
Secretary, Department of Land Resources (DoLR), Shri Narendra Bhooshan, delivered the welcome address and set the context for the guidelines, noting that DILRMP 3.0 marks a shift toward building an integrated Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) for land administration. Joint Secretary (LR), Shri Parikipandla Narahari, gave a comprehensive presentation detailing the technical architecture and scheme components.
Key Highlights of DILRMP 3.0
GIS-enabled ‘Land Stack’:
Land Stack, an integrated digital framework would bring together different layers of land-related information such as georeferenced cadastral maps, Records of Rights, property registrations, and relevant court matters through GIS based digital interfaces. It will enable different land-related systems to be connected and accessed in an interoperable manner, while allowing each State to develop its own Land Stack by integrating its various land-related datasets and systems through APIs. These State-level Land Stacks would, in turn, form the building blocks of a
National Land Stack
, which would be developed in a federated manner, enabling seamless interoperability and exchange of information across States while retaining the respective ownership and control of data with the concerned authorities.
Universal Bhu-Aadhaar (ULPIN):
Assigns a 14-digit unique identifier to every land parcel in the country to establish unambiguous property identities and eliminate fraud.
Registration Seva Kendras (RSKs):
High-footfall 75 Sub-Registrar Offices will be modernized into citizen-friendly service centers with digital queue management and improved amenities, drawing inspiration from Passport Seva Kendras.
Scanning of Legacy Records:
Historical land and property registration records will be systematically scanned and digitally archived to protect inheritance rights and curb ancestral land disputes.
Registration Repository:
A secure digital framework of registered deeds and encumbrance information to enable ownership verification, transaction history and property due diligence.
Paperless Revenue Courts:
Modernizes the Revenue Court Case Management System (RCCMS) by linking it directly with land records to cut case pendency and expedite mutation settlements.
Urban Land Mapping (NAKSHA):
Accelerates the NAKSHA pilot project to create accurate, GIS-based urban land records and issue Urban Property Cards (UrPro Cards).
Implementation and Monitoring
DILRMP 3.0 will be implemented across all States and Union Territories with 100% central funding under a phased, performance-linked mechanism managed through the Public Financial Management System (PFMS). Progress will be monitored in real time via an upgraded DILRMP-MIS dashboard overseen by the Project Sanctioning & Monitoring Committee (PS&MC). The event concluded with a vote of thanks proposed by the Director, DoLR.

title: Upcoming ESTIC-2026 (Emerging Science, Technology & Innovation Conclave) to be held from 27–29 October 2026 at Bharat Mandapam Delhi with inauguration by PM Shri Narendra Modi; faculty to include three Nobel Laureates and several international award-winning speakers: Dr Jitendra Singh
subtitle:
ESTIC was conceived last year as part of a new approach to bring together multiple components of the science and technology ecosystem on a common platform rather than having several fragmented events throughout the year, says the Minister.

50-60 percent of Startups are now coming from small towns and not metros; they greater access to experts, entrepreneurs, business leaders and markets to scale up: Dr Jitendra Singh

India’s Next Innovation Wave Must Come from Beyond Metros: Union Minister Dr Jitendra Singh

Break Silos, Build Bridges from Labs to Markets: Dr Jitendra Singh Calls for Stronger Research-Startup-Industry Connect at ESTIC-2026 Curtain Raiser event

Dr Jitendra Singh also emphasises Wider Integration of Management, Communication with Science to Scale Innovation

Dr Jitendra Singh Seeks ESTIC Roadmap with Short- and Long-Term Milestones, Says Conclave Must Go Beyond Stand-alone Annual Event
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                10 SEP 2026 5:02PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences, and MoS PMO, Personnel, Public Grievances, Pensions, Atomic Energy and Space, Dr. Jitendra Singh, today disclosed that ESTIC-2026 (Emerging Science, Technology & Innovation Conclave) will be held from 27–29 October 2026 at Bharat Mandapam with inauguration by PM Shri Narendra Modi and the eminent faculty will include three Nobel Laureates, Prof. Joachim Frank, Sir Richard J. Roberts and Prof. Kostya Novoselov, in addition to several international award winning speakers.
Addressing the Curtain Raiser of ESTIC-2026, Dr. Jitendra Singh said that with science and technology evolving at unprecedented speed, the ecosystem must increasingly draw upon expertise from management, communication and other domains alongside scientific capabilities.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said ESTIC was conceived last year as part of a new approach to bring together multiple components of the science and technology ecosystem on a common platform rather than having several fragmented events throughout the year. He said the Conclave provides an opportunity for closer interaction among researchers, innovators, Startups, entrepreneurs, industry and policymakers, with the objective of creating a more integrated ecosystem for science and technology.
The Minister said, time has come for breaking institutional silos and creating stronger linkages between scientific research, Startups, industry, markets and society to accelerate innovation and translate India’s scientific capabilities into wider economic and societal impact.
Dr Jitendra Singh said the theme of ESTIC-2026: “Creative Minds, Catalyzing Science, Empowering Technologies”, captures the importance of creativity and imagination in scientific innovation. Dr. Singh said creativity and imagination strengthen innovative capabilities, while an enabling ecosystem is necessary to translate ideas into meaningful outcomes.
Referring to India’s startup growth, Dr. Jitendra Singh said the country had around 350-400 Startups in 2014, whereas the number has now crossed 2.3 lakh, making India the world’s third-largest startup ecosystem. He said more than 50-60 per cent of Startups are now coming from small towns and not metros, reflecting the widening reach of entrepreneurship and innovation across the country. He said such emerging Startups deserve greater access to experts, entrepreneurs, business leaders and markets to scale up.
The Minister said future editions of ESTIC could bring in management and communication institutions more extensively. Management expertise can help Startups and potential entrepreneurs develop strategies for market access, while communication expertise can help take scientific achievements to young people and wider sections of society through the language and mediums they understand.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said the Government’s efforts to create such an enabling ecosystem include initiatives such as the National Research Foundation and the ₹1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund. He said the convergence of different ministries and stakeholders can help strengthen the journey from research and innovation to technology development, entrepreneurship and market applications.
The Minister also referred to India’s recent achievements in emerging areas of science and technology, including the Deep Ocean Mission and the country’s expanding focus on the blue economy. Referring to the launch of India’s first indigenous research vessel, he said India is now moving in a major way to explore the opportunities offered by the blue economy. He also cited achievements in space and biotechnology as examples of the scale of India’s expanding scientific capabilities.
Calling for continuity beyond the three-day Conclave, Dr. Singh asked the scientific advisory and organising teams to prepare a roadmap with short-term and long-term milestones based on the deliberations and learnings of ESTIC. He said the experience of one edition should feed into the next and that inter-ministerial efforts should continue so that the Conclave does not become an isolated annual event.
Dr. Jitendra Singh also called for greater awareness among young innovators about procedures related to startup registration, patents and other innovation processes. He said many potential entrepreneurs may possess ideas and capabilities but remain unfamiliar with the procedures required to take their innovations forward, and that easier access to such information can help unlock this potential.
Speaking about the rapidly evolving technology landscape, particularly Artificial Intelligence, the Minister said technology is increasingly becoming a facilitator for young people to create new possibilities, rather than merely seek opportunities created by technology. He said ESTIC should become an event of interest to every generation and segment of society, particularly the youth.
The Curtain Raiser was attended by Prof. Ajay K. Sood, Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India; Dr. N. Kalaiselvi, Secretary, Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) and Director General, CSIR; Dr. Rajesh S. Gokhale, Secretary, Department of Biotechnology; Shri S. Krishnan, Secretary, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology; and Dr. Parvinder Maini, Scientific Secretary, Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser, besides senior officials and representatives of participating ministries and departments.
Prof. Ajay K. Sood, Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India, said ESTIC-2026 builds on the success of its inaugural edition, which brought together 13 ministries, leading institutions, industry partners and more than 5,000 delegates. He said the Conclave embodies a whole-of-government approach and brings together young innovators, policymakers, institutions and industry around a common national vision, with 12 thematic areas covering important emerging opportunities for India.
Dr. N. Kalaiselvi, Secretary, DSIR & Director General, CSIR, said CSIR has taken up the responsibility of organising ESTIC-2026, with CSIR-NIIST, Thiruvananthapuram, as the nodal laboratory, and 13 ministries joining hands for the initiative. She said the Conclave will strengthen coordination across the science, technology and innovation ecosystem and contribute to the national objective of building Viksit Bharat by 2047.
ESTIC-2026, organised by CSIR under the guidance of the Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India, with CSIR-NIIST as the organising partner, will bring together Nobel laureates and global scientific leaders, deep-tech Startups, women entrepreneurs, young scientists and researchers, industry leaders, policymakers and representatives from academia, PSUs and R&D institutions.
The three-day Conclave will feature plenary talks, 12 thematic technical sessions, panel discussions, presentations by science and technology leaders and deep-tech Startups, exhibitions, poster presentations and B2B/B2G connect meetings. The thematic areas span emerging fields including advanced manufacturing, energy technologies, synthetic biology, ocean and maritime technologies, quantum communication, semiconductors, agri-tech, generative and autonomous AI, robotics, advanced healthcare, immersive technologies and space science.
Three Nobel laureates: Prof. Joachim Frank, Sir Richard J. Roberts and Prof. Kostya Novoselov, are among the eminent scientific personalities participating in ESTIC-2026. The Conclave will also feature a technology-oriented exhibition showcasing India’s emerging startup and deep-tech ecosystem, which will be open to the public from the second day.
ESTIC-2026 will be held from 27–29 October 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi. The Hon’ble Prime Minister of India will inaugurate ESTIC-2026 on 27 October 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi. Registration is open and will close on 15 September 2026.

title: Sediments from Bakhira Lake can help water resource management in the Central Ganga Plain
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                10 SEP 2026 4:41PM by PIB Delhi
content:
A new study that measured magnetic minerals accumulated in sediments below the Bakhira Lake in Sant Kabir Nagar over 25000 years helped track past changes in climate and how they have influenced rainfall, weathering, sediment transport and lake processes in northern India.
It can pave way for improved climate models to predict future monsoon behaviour and can help better water resource management in the Central Ganga Plain (CGP) of which the Bakhira Lake is a part.
The CGP is one of the most important regions influenced by the Indian Summer Monsoon and is critical in terms of agricultural practices.
Long-term, high-resolution palaeoclimate records from the CGP region are scarce. Most previous studies focused on biological proxies or covered only the Holocene period.
In order to respond to this gap, researchers of Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences (BSIP), an autonomous institute of the Department of Science and Technology (DST), investigated the potential of environmental magnetic properties preserved in the sediments of Bakhira Lake could provide a continuous and reliable archive of monsoon variability earlier than Holocene i.e. since the Last Glacial Maximum.
Bakhira Lake is located in the Ghaghara–Rapti alluvial system and represents a perennial oxbow/floodplain wetland formed through the migration and subsequent cut-off of the Rapti River. One of the largest wetlands in Uttar Pradesh, it was designated as a Ramsar Site in 2022
.
Its floodplain–lacustrine setting favours the accumulation and preservation of sediments derived from both the lake and surrounding catchment, making it sensitive to changes in monsoon-driven runoff, sediment transport and weathering. In addition, the Bakhira sediment sequence extends back to approximately 25 ka and is constrained by seven accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) radiocarbon dates
,
providing a comparatively well-dated terrestrial archive for investigating Late Quaternary environmental and climatic variability in the CGP.
Environmental magnetic measurements from this lake could provide valuable proxies for reconstructing past climatic and environmental changes by recording variations in hydrology, erosion, sediment input and pedogenic processes
.
The availability of a well-preserved sediment sequence and complementary multiproxy datasets further encouraged this investigation.
Using environmental magnetic properties integrated with grain-size, geochemical and clay mineralogical records, Nazakat Ali, Sajid Ali, Biswajeet Thakur, Anupam Sharma reconstructed variations in the Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) from the Last Glacial Maximum to the present.
The record identifies major climatic events, including the Last Glacial Maximum, Heinrich Stadial 1 (LGM; ~25.3–18.1 cal ka BP marked by cold and dry conditions with a weakened Indian Summer Monsoon -ISM), Bølling–Allerød (B/A; ~15.3–12.8 cal ka BP, a relatively warm and humid interval associated with enhanced ISM activity), Younger Dryas (YD; ~12.8–11.1 cal ka BP characterised by renewed cooling, drying and weakened monsoon conditions) Holocene Climatic Optimum (HCO; ~9.2–4 cal ka BP, when warmer and wetter conditions prevailed, accompanied by enhanced monsoon precipitation and pedogenic activity) and late Holocene droughts (~4–2 cal ka BP reflects a period of relatively dry conditions and reduced monsoon strength) and demonstrates how these events influenced rainfall, weathering, sediment transport and lake processes in northern India.
Fig. 1
Location and geomorphological setting of Bakhira Lake, showing the sampling site, surrounding drainage network, major geomorphic units, and regional elevation.
By combining seven AMS radiocarbon dates with multiple environmental magnetic parameters and integrating them with previously published sedimentological and geochemical datasets from the same core, this study provides a robust reconstruction of long-term Indian Summer Monsoon variability which key focus for changing climate scenario in present and our agricultural dominated system.
This research published in Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology improves our understanding of how the Indian Summer Monsoon has responded to natural climate change much before the instrumental record where direct evidence for climate change is relied upon proxy-based research. Such long-term records are essential for distinguishing natural climate variability from recent human-induced climate change.
The findings provide valuable baseline information for improving climate models, predicting future monsoon behaviour, and understanding the response of river and lake systems to changing rainfall patterns. The study also supports better planning for water-resource management, agriculture, flood and drought mitigation, and environmental conservation in the Ganga Plain, where millions of people depend directly on monsoon rainfall.
Publication link:
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.palaeo.2026.114028

title: India Charts Course to Become Global Hub for Ship Ownership, Leasing and Maritime Finance: Sarbananda Sonowal

GIFT City Emerges as the Enabling Platform for India's Maritime Finance Ambitions

Sonowal Addressed the India Ship Leasing and Financing Summit at the IFSC in GIFT City
ministry: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                10 SEP 2026 6:48PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of Ports, Shipping & Waterways, Sarbananda Sonowal, was the Chief Guest at the India Ship Leasing and Financing Summit, organised by the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) in collaboration with the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW), at the GIFT City Club, Gandhinagar, today.
The summit brought together policymakers, ship owners, lessors, charterers, financiers and maritime stakeholders to deliberate on India's push to build a comprehensive ship ownership, leasing and financing ecosystem, with GIFT City positioned as the platform enabling this ambition.
Addressing the gathering, Sonowal invoked India's maritime legacy, tracing it to the Indus Valley Civilization and the ancient port of Lothal in Gujarat. "This gathering marks a significant milestone in our collective journey to position India, and particularly GIFT City, as a global maritime hub for a comprehensive maritime value chain ecosystem
,
encompassing ship leasing, owning, financing, insurance, brokering and other ancillary services," Sonowal said.
The Minister pointed to India's growing fleet footprint, with 38 ship lessors now registered and collectively leasing 43 vessels, taking total leasing capacity past 2.99 million DWT, of which 24 vessels now fly the Indian flag. He added that 41 domestic and international banks have set up in the IFSC, extending close to USD 60.1 million in funding to ship leasing entities, with DGMA's first regional office opening in GIFT City set to further strengthen this ecosystem for shipowners and operators.
Sonowal outlined key reforms enabling Indian shipping to compete globally, including exemption from licensing requirements under the Coastal Shipping Act, 2025, for foreign vessels on charter, and permission for GIFT IFSC-based shipping companies to own foreign-flag vessels. On the latter, Sonowal said, "More fundamentally, it marks a shift in how we count our fleet
,

title: From Need to Opportunity: DEPwD, ALIMCO and EkStep Join Hands to Build a Digital Bridge for Persons with Disabilities
date:

                10 SEP 2026 6:12PM by PIB Delhi
content:
A new digital architecture is set to bring Persons with Disabilities (PwDs) and the opportunities, services and support they need closer than ever. The Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD), Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment, Artificial Limbs Manufacturing Corporation of India (ALIMCO) and EkStep Foundation, Bengaluru, today signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in New Delhi to establish an institutional framework for the design, development, implementation and scaling of the
Purple Dots – UBI (Unified Benefits Interface) Initiative
.
Conceptualised by DEPwD, the Purple Dots Initiative seeks to address a fundamental challenge in disability inclusion—not merely the availability of benefits and services, but the ability of a person to discover the right opportunity, service or support at the right time and place. At its core, a “Purple Dot” is a simple digital profile through which a Person with Disability can indicate who they are and what they need—whether it is employment, assistive technology such as a wheelchair, skill development, training or any other support. Similarly, employers, service providers, NGOs, philanthropic organisations and other institutions can create their own “dots” to indicate the opportunities, services and resources they offer.
By bringing these dots together through an open and interoperable digital infrastructure, the initiative seeks to create a connected ecosystem in which needs and opportunities can discover each other locally and efficiently. An open digital protocol will enable ecosystem stakeholders to interact and respond to identified needs in real time, helping move disability inclusion from fragmented access towards seamless discovery, linkage and participation.
The MoU establishes a collaborative framework for taking the Purple Dots – UBI (Unified Benefits Interface) Initiative from concept to implementation and scale. It envisages enabling Persons with Disabilities to discover and connect with relevant government entitlements, services, employment opportunities, training programmes, assistive devices and support systems offered by Government Departments, private-sector entities, civil society organisations, NGOs, philanthropic institutions and other ecosystem partners.
The initiative represents a significant step towards strengthening accessibility and inclusion through digital public infrastructure. Rather than creating isolated systems for individual schemes or institutions, Purple Dots seeks to enable different actors in the disability ecosystem to connect and collaborate through an interoperable framework, thereby improving the visibility and reach of services and opportunities that are already available.
EkStep Foundation, a philanthropy instrumental in conceiving and architecting Digital Public Infrastructure/ Digital Public Good initiatives for large-scale societal transformation, is partnering with DEPwD and ALIMCO to bring its experience of building open and collaborative digital ecosystems to the disability sector. The partnership seeks to strengthen the ability of local ecosystem players to discover one another and connect Persons with Disabilities with relevant services, opportunities and support, building on capabilities that already exist across the country.
The collaboration brings together the mandate and nationwide reach of DEPwD, the experience and capabilities of ALIMCO in the disability sector, and EkStep Foundation’s experience in enabling ecosystem-led digital innovation at scale. Together, the partners seek to make support and services more accessible, discoverable and connected for Persons with Disabilities across districts, while strengthening the participation of Government, industry, civil society and other stakeholders in creating an inclusive ecosystem.
The MoU-signing ceremony was attended by Ms. Manmeet Kaur Nanda, Additional Secretary; Shri Ashish Thakre, Director; Shri Pradeep A., Director; and Shri Sandeep Kumar, Under Secretary, from DEPwD. From ALIMCO, Shri Pankaj Dwivedi, Assistant Manager; and Ms. Priya Grover, Assistant Manager, were present. Shri Ikpreet Singh, Director; Shri Gaurav Gupta represented EkStep Foundation, Bengaluru.
The Purple Dots Initiative envisages a future in which a person’s need does not remain invisible and an available opportunity does not remain undiscovered—where digital connectivity becomes a practical bridge between Persons with Disabilities and the ecosystem of services, opportunities and support around them.
This version deliberately uses
“Need to make Opportunity visible and localize”
as the news hook, making the Purple Dots concept understandable to a general newspaper reader rather than presenting the MoU merely as an institutional agreement.

title: From Alcohol Dependence to Renewed Stability: Kavi's Journey towards Recovery, Responsibility and Hope
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                10 SEP 2026 3:13PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Alcohol dependence can gradually affect an individual's physical health, emotional well-being, family relationships and ability to maintain a stable livelihood. Timely counselling, structured rehabilitation and sustained family support can help individuals overcome dependency and rebuild their lives with confidence and dignity.
Demonstrating the impact of support under the National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction (NAPDDR), Kavi (name changed), a 31-year-old resident of Erode district in Tamil Nadu, has overcome nearly six years of alcohol dependence and is now leading a healthier and more stable life.
His journey reflects the role of counselling, rehabilitation and continuous follow-up in enabling lasting recovery.
Kavi, who belongs to the General category, studied up to high school and works as a full-time employee. What began as occasional drinking gradually developed into dependency as he attempted to cope with emotional stress, family pressure and personal disappointments.
Over time, alcohol dependence adversely affected his physical health, emotional well-being, relationships and ability to manage daily responsibilities. He experienced emotional instability, disturbed sleep, reduced motivation and loss of self-confidence, leaving him increasingly isolated and uncertain about his future.
His family became deeply concerned as they witnessed his emotional outbursts and withdrawal from social interactions. Alcohol dependence also affected his attendance and performance at work, making it difficult for him to maintain a stable income and manage his finances. This added to the emotional and economic strain experienced by the family.
Despite these challenges, Kavi remained determined to change his life. On 7 October 2025, he received support from the Centre for Action and Rural Education, an Integrated Rehabilitation Centre for Addicts (IRCA) in Erode district, Tamil Nadu.
Under a structured recovery plan, Kavi received individual counselling, emotional and psychological support, family counselling, motivational and behavioural guidance, relapse-prevention education and regular follow-up monitoring. The programme also focused on emotional regulation, healthy coping strategies, group therapy, family involvement and lifestyle modification.
Kavi actively participated in the rehabilitation programme and demonstrated a strong commitment to recovery and personal growth. Continuous counselling helped him understand the impact of alcohol dependence, manage stress more effectively and adopt healthier ways of responding to emotional challenges.
With sustained guidance and family support, he gradually regained confidence and emotional stability. He rebuilt healthy relationships with his family members and became more responsible in managing his daily routine and professional commitments.
The recovery process also brought positive changes to his employment and financial condition. Improved attendance, work performance and financial management strengthened his earning capacity and contributed to greater economic stability for his family.
At present, Kavi is maintaining sobriety and leading a healthier, more stable and productive life. He continues to attend follow-up counselling sessions and remains committed to sustaining his recovery. His transformation has also become a source of encouragement for others facing similar challenges.
Kavi's journey demonstrates that alcohol dependence can be overcome through determination, appropriate treatment, family participation and sustained institutional support. With renewed confidence and responsibility, he has moved towards a life of dignity, economic stability and hope.

title: First-ever district-level estimates released by NSO for unincorporated non-agricultural sector
subtitle:
Top 50 districts drive nearly one-third of the sector’s activity

Women comprise one-third of workforce in 237 districts
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                10 SEP 2026 4:00PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Snapshot:
NSO disseminates district-level estimates from a large-scale, nation-wide enterprise survey for the first time, marking a significant step towards strengthening granular sub-state-level statistics in India.
The top 50 districts, ranked by the number of unincorporated establishments, account for nearly one-third of the total establishments, workforce and Gross Value Added.
Roughly one-third of all districts have more than one lakh unincorporated establishments per district.
In 237 districts, women constitute one-third of the total workforce in the unincorporated sector.
In 280 districts, GVA per worker exceeds the all-India average indicating relatively higher levels of economic productivity in these districts.
NSO Releases insights on urban unincorporated enterprise landscape at district level
The importance of granular and high-frequency data has grown significantly in recent years, reflecting the increasing need for evidence-based policymaking and targeted interventions. In particular, sub-state-level statistics play a crucial role in identifying regional variations, emerging strengths and areas requiring attention, thereby enabling more targeted and area-specific policy interventions.
As part of this endeavour, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) has already published, for the first time, a comprehensive statistical profile of the unincorporated sector across the country’s 46 million-plus cities, identified on the basis of Census 2011 population. Taking this initiative further, MoSPI has now presented a district-level portrait of the scale, structure and economic performance of India’s unincorporated non-agricultural sector across States and Union Territories (UTs). The district-level estimates presented in this report also include the corresponding estimates for million-plus cities located within the respective districts. This marks the first initiative of the National Statistics Office (NSO), MoSPI, to disseminate district-level estimates from a large-scale, nationwide survey. The report is available on the website of the Ministry at
https://mospi.gov.in
.
Unincorporated Sector at the District Level: Insights from ASUSE 2025
Drawing upon ASUSE 2025 data, this report presents a comprehensive picture of the unincorporated sector at the district level through a balanced set of indicators covering the scale and structure of establishments, employment and emoluments, and economic performance. These include estimates of establishments and workers, ownership and employment structure, women’s participation, registration status, emoluments per hired worker, and GVA per establishment and GVA per worker for market establishments. Estimates of these indicators are given for 757 out of 770 districts available in the sampling frame during sample selection of ASUSE 2025 offering granular district-level insights based on nationally representative survey data. However, the geographical coverage of some districts and number of districts may differ from the current administrative configuration due to subsequent changes in district boundaries, names and/or the creation of new districts.
As Lakshadweep and Chandigarh each comprise only one district, the district-level estimates for these UTs coincide with their respective UT-level estimates and already published in the ASUSE 2025 report. Accordingly, separate district-level estimates are not presented for Lakshadweep and Chandigarh in this report. Additionally, owing to the very small rural population and the limited number of villages in Delhi, all districts were combined into a single stratum for the rural sector, from which the sample FSUs were selected. A similar approach was adopted for the urban sector. Accordingly, district-level estimates for Delhi could not be generated and, therefore, are not presented in this Report.
A brief overview of the coverage, sampling methodology, and data collection mechanism of ASUSE 2025 are provided in the Endnote.
Insight from Unincorporated Enterprise Landscape
Geographical concentration and district-level dynamics of the unincorporated sector
The unincorporated non-agricultural sector exhibits a notable concentration of economic activity across districts. The top 10 districts, ranked by the estimated number of unincorporated establishments, together account for about one-tenth of the total establishments, workers and Gross Value Added (GVA) generated by the sector while the top 50 districts capture nearly one-third of the total establishments, workforce and GVA.
The top 10 districts are spread across four States: Gujarat, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal, while the top 50 districts are spread across twelve states viz. Bihar, Gujarat, Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra, Odisha, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal.
The district-level distribution further reveals considerable variation in the scale of the unincorporated sector across the country. Roughly one-third of all districts have more than one lakh unincorporated
establishments per district, while about 9% of the districts have fewer than 10,000 establishments per district. Only 16 districts (eight from West Bengal, three from Maharashtra, two from Gujarat, one each from Karnataka, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh) have more than 5 lakh unincorporated establishments per district.
Productivity performance across districts
District-level estimates also highlight variations in the productivity performance of the unincorporated sector. In about 331 districts, GVA per worker is estimated to be between ₹1 lakh and ₹1.5 lakh. In 280 districts, GVA per worker exceeds the all-India average (Rs. 1,56,539) indicating relatively higher levels of economic productivity in these districts.
District-level landscape of female entrepreneurship
The district-level estimates reveal significant regional patterns in female entrepreneurship. The top 10 districts with the highest share of female-led unincorporated establishments are located in Telangana, Manipur and Meghalaya. In Mizoram, female-owned proprietary establishments account for at least 50 per cent of establishments in each district of the State.
A similar pattern is observed in the participation of women in the workforce. Top ten districts with the highest share of female workers are located in Telangana, Manipur, Meghalaya and Mizoram, reflecting the significant role played by women in the unincorporated sector in these states. In as many as 237 districts, women constitute one-third of the total workforce in the unincorporated sector whereas in 25 districts the female workers constitute more than 50% of the workforce.

A brief about the coverage, sampling scheme, and data collection mechanism in the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE):
A. Coverage
:
A.1. Geographically,
the survey
covers the rural and urban areas of whole of India (except some of the villages in Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are difficult to access).
A.2. Sector-wise, this survey captures unincorporated non-agricultural establishments belonging to three sectors viz., Manufacturing, Trade and Other Services.
A.3. Ownership-wise, unincorporated non-agricultural establishments pertaining to proprietorship, partnership (excluding Limited Liability Partnerships), co-operatives, societies/trusts etc. have been covered
in this survey
.
B. Sampling Scheme
:
The survey has been conducted following a multi-stage stratified sampling scheme, where first stage units (FSUs) are census villages in rural area (except for rural Kerala, where Panchayat wards have been taken as FSUs) and UFS (Urban Frame Survey) blocks in urban areas which are updated periodically. The ultimate stage units (USUs) are establishments for both the sectors. In the case of large FSUs, one intermediate stage of sampling has been done in the form of hamlet groups in rural and sub-blocks in urban.
Due to very small population size and very few villages in rural sector of Delhi, all the districts in Delhi were merged into one stratum only and sample FSUs in rural areas were selected from that stratum. In urban areas also, same treatment was given. Hence, for Delhi, district level estimates cannot be generated and presented in this Report.
D
.
Data Collection Mechanism
:
The survey has been conducted based on area frame and establishments have been listed in the selected FSUs of both rural and urban sector and from the listed establishments in the FSUs
, requisite number of establishments were surveyed as per the sampling design. Mostly, data were collected from the selected establishments through oral enquiry pertaining to the ‘monthly’ reference period.
The data for the survey were collected in Tablet using Computer Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI).
E. Note to users and caveats:
The district-level estimates are based on sample survey data and should be interpreted taking into account the differences across regions arising out of underlying economic and demographic characteristics, variations in industrial composition, local conditions, and sampling variability. To facilitate informed use of the estimates, measures of statistical reliability, in terms of Relative Standard Errors (RSEs) has been provided. In some cases, the Relative Standard Errors (RSEs) presented in this report are high and such cases may be duly considered while drawing inferences.
The report on
Unincorporated Sector at the District Level: Insights from ASUSE 2025
is available on the website of the ministry (
https://www.mospi.gov.in
). Scan the QR code to access the Publications/Reports.

title: First Regional Review Conference on Implementation of the Forest Rights Act Held in Bengaluru
subtitle: Southern States apprise Ministry of Tribal Affairs of progress in disposal of claims, recognition of Community Forest Rights and Habitat Rights; time-bound roadmaps called for
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                10 SEP 2026 7:39PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Tribal Affairs (MoTA), Government of India, convened the first Regional Review Conference on implementation of the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA) at Bengaluru, Karnataka, today, bringing together senior functionaries of the Tribal Welfare, Revenue and Forest Departments of the five Southern States, namely Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Telangana, to review the status of implementation and deliberate upon a coordinated way forward.
Proceedings commenced with a Welcome Address by the Secretary, Scheduled Tribes Welfare Department, Government of Karnataka, who apprised the gathering of the objectives of the Conference and extended a formal welcome to the dignitaries and delegates, followed by a presentation of traditional tribal dance by artistes representing the tribal communities of Karnataka. This was followed by the Keynote Address of the Joint Secretary, MoTA, and the Special Address of the Secretary, MoTA. The Joint Secretary apprised the Conference that, as on 30 June 2026, over 54 lakh Individual Forest Rights (IFR) claims have been received nationally, with approximately 25.42 lakh titles distributed over nearly 238 lakh acres, while over 10 lakh claims remain pending and 19,845 Community Forest Rights (CFR) stand recognised; the Southern States were called upon to accord priority to time-bound disposal of pending claims, recognition of Community Forest Resource Rights and Habitat Rights of Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs), and incorporation of recognised rights in land records. In her Special Address, the Secretary, MoTA, underscored that recognition of rights must translate into tenure security, sustainable livelihoods and convergence with development schemes, leading to the empowerment of tribal communities. The Secretary called for greater attention to Community Forest Rights and Community Forest Resource Rights, noting their potential to strengthen Gram Sabha-led forest governance and community-based livelihoods, and referred to the recent joint advisory issued by MoTA and the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change enabling integration of Community Forest Resource Management Plans with Forest Department working and management plans. Underlining that habitat rights of PVTGs embody living systems of culture, livelihood and traditional knowledge, the Secretary called for their recognition to be undertaken with sensitivity and active community participation.
The Director, FRA, MoTA, apprised the Conference of the national scenario of FRA implementation, with particular focus on progress made by the Southern States, covering issues such as pendency of claims, incorporation of Records of Rights, recognition of Habitat Rights, recognition of Community Forest Resource Rights (CFRR), and the support being extended by the Ministry in this regard. The Deputy Secretary, MoTA, thereafter apprised the Conference of the need for digitisation of FRA records and introduced the National-level FRA Portal, currently under development, and urged States to utilise the Portal and integrate their existing FRA records through Application Programming Interface (API).
State-wise Presentations
Officers of the five Southern States thereafter apprised the Conference of the status of FRA implementation in their respective States, as summarised below:
Karnataka: Of 2,95,176 applications received, 16,700 Forest Rights Titles have been distributed and 15,553 claims remain under verification; delay in constitution of Taluk and Zilla Panchayats has affected functioning of the Sub-Divisional and District Level Committees, and re-verification of rejected claims through 'Mahajaru' committees is under progress, with FRA beneficiary data being integrated with the State's FRUITS and Bhoomi platforms for scheme convergence.
Tamil Nadu: 15,838 titles issued in Phase-I stand digitised, while 41,692 fresh claims received under Phase-II are under verification, supported by a State-wide FRA Atlas, dedicated District FRA Cells and structured capacity-building of Forest Rights Committees.
Andhra Pradesh: As on 31 August 2026, 2,27,300 Individual and 1,225 Community titles stand distributed against 2,90,874 claims received, with an integrated land-record and welfare-delivery model linking the Giribhumi FRA portal with the State's revenue and banking systems.
Telangana: 2,30,735 Individual and 102 Community titles have been distributed against 6,55,249 claims received, supported by a fully digitised Online RoFR Title Granting System integrated with the BhuBharathi revenue portal, conferred the SKOCH Award of Excellence (Gold, 2024).
Kerala: 29,545 Individual and 286 Community titles have been recognised, with pendency of 1,616 individual and 108 community claims attributed mainly to survey and verification processes, and six Forest Villages converted into Revenue Villages.
Way Forward
The Ministry called upon the Southern States to ensure time-bound disposal and reconciliation of pending and rejected claims, accelerate recognition of Community Forest Resource Rights and PVTG Habitat Rights, complete incorporation of recognised rights in revenue and forest records, and strengthen convergence with livelihood and welfare schemes, with State-specific roadmaps and timelines which were worked out by the respective States.

content:
Shri Rajiv Gauba, Member, NITI Aayog, participated in a fireside chat on "From Regulation to Transformation: Building India's Next-Generation Reform Architecture" at the Global Fintech Fest 2026, a conversation spanning India's regulatory journey, the need for balance between innovation and oversight in fintech, and the institutional changes needed to sustain growth to achieve the Viksit Bharat vision.
Reflecting on the reforms of the past decade, Shri Gauba noted that measures such as the Goods and Services Tax, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, and a liberalized foreign investment regime had reshaped the economy and opened up sectors once considered off-limits to private enterprise, including defence, space and now nuclear energy.
He said the next-generation reform architecture should be defined by “deregulation”, with the focus on “nuts-and-bolts” reform, on doing away with the license – approval –permission and frequent renewals regime that prevails in different avatars. He emphasised the need to systematically review laws, regulations and administrative processes. This work, he said, is being carried out by a High-Level Committee, guided by the philosophy of Trust Based Governance espoused by the Prime Minister.
Many important reforms, he noted, fall in the domain of States and municipal governments and pointed to the work being done by the Deregulation Task Force, carrying the Trust-Based Governance principles down to the State and city level. Citing the scheme for Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment and the Urban Challenge Fund, he characterized the Center Governments approach as "cooperative federalism with a competitive edge", where scheme incentives are linked to reform milestones and projects are selected through challenge mode.
On fintech, Shri Gauba highlighted India’s phenomenal growth in the sector and how it has contributed to financial inclusion and access. He cited India's digital public infrastructure - from Aadhaar and UPI to DigiLocker and the account aggregator framework – as a model that the world can replicate, where Governments lays open, secure and interoperable rails on which private enterprise builds and innovates. He said regulation in technology-driven sectors should strike a dynamic balance between protecting public interest and allowing innovation to flourish. Regulatory frameworks, he added, should be principles-based, technology-neutral and proportionate to risk, while promoting competition, ensuring non-discriminatory access to underlying infrastructure and improving information symmetry. He also emphasised the need for greater coordination among financial regulators, simpler and more predictable compliance processes, and continued efforts to reduce frictions and interoperability gaps.
Shri Gauba noted the steps taken by the Government to attract long-term domestic and foreign capital, by improving investor confidence in aspects of fair treatment, predictable policy, strong data governance, cybersecurity, and adequate space for innovation.
Concluding his remarks, Shri Gauba said reform has to be an integral part of the culture of governance, supported by long-term and strategic thinking. Prime Minister’s call for Viksit Bharat by 2047 to be approached as a national enterprise, with government, industry and citizens each playing an important role in sustaining India’s reform and growth momentum.

title: BRICS
subtitle: Evolution, Cooperation and India's Leadership
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                10 SEP 2026 12:43PM by PIB Delhi
content:
A boardroom acronym for four emerging markets has grown into something far bigger. Today It is a geopolitical bloc spanning four continents. The journey runs from a four-country dialogue to today's far wider grouping. Successive waves of membership pulled in oil states, African economies and Southeast Asian partners. At the centre of this expanding architecture sits India this year, chairing the grouping for a fourth time since its inception.
BRICS: Shaping an Inclusive Global Order
BRICS has emerged as a key platform for coordinating economic policy among major emerging economies. It serves as the principal forum where these nations shape a common position on global governance. Through sustained dialogue, it has become a channel for advancing the interests of the Global South within multilateral institutions. Its agenda spans development, finance, technology, trade and people-to-people exchanges.
The grouping reflects the growing economic weight and aspirations of emerging economies globally.
It provides members with a platform to share experiences and address common challenges.
Under its 2026 Presidency,
India is set to host the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on 12–13 September 2026.
It will mark India’s fourth Chairship of BRICS in 2026. India’s Chairship is guided by the theme
“Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.
” The theme reflects India’s focus on strengthening existing achievements and institutional effectiveness. It places development, sustainability and innovation at the heart of the agenda. It also highlights the aspirations of the Global South. India seeks to reinforce BRICS as a constructive and solutions-oriented forum.
Today, BRICS comprises
11 countries
:
Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE
. Collectively, these members represent
49.5% of the global population, 40% of global GDP, and 26% of global trade
. These figures underline their substantial demographic and economic weight. Its expanded membership has also widened its geographical reach across Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America.
This diversity brings together major markets, natural resources, technological capabilities and varied development experiences.
The Origin
The acronym
‘BRIC’ was coined in 2001 by Goldman Sachs
in its Global Economics Paper,
‘The World Needs Better Economic BRICs.’
Based on econometric analysis, the paper projected that
Brazil, Russia, India and China
would be among the world’s largest economies over the following five decades. Their growing economic weight and vast geographic reach across three continents highlighted their emerging global significance.
The BRIC concept subsequently evolved into a formal grouping, with South Africa joining in 2010 and transforming BRIC into BRICS.
The evolution marked the transition from an economic grouping identified by analysts to a formal platform for political, economic and development cooperation
.
The Aim, Objective and Areas of Cooperation
BRICS was initially conceived as a forum for dialogue on major issues shaping the international agenda. Its early focus was on developing common positions on global political and economic matters. It sought to promote a more democratic, legitimate and balanced international order.
The grouping also emphasised sustainable economic and social development, social inclusion and shared prosperity among emerging economies.
Over time, these priorities have provided a foundation for deeper and broader engagement among members.
Across successive summits, BRICS cooperation has progressively expanded to encompass strategic global issues and areas of practical collaboration.
Its agenda covers terrorism, climate change, food and energy security, trade and agriculture.
It also addresses labour and employment, telecommunications, international finance and the global economic situation.
BRICS advocates for greater representation and equity in international institutions, including the WTO and global financial architecture.
These efforts seek to make global governance more inclusive, effective and responsive to contemporary challenges.
BRICS Through the Years:
From Crisis to Collective Action
The
2008 global financial crisis
marked a defining moment in the evolution of BRICS. It exposed gaps in the existing global financial architecture. It also created a need for broader consensus on global economic governance. The four BRIC countries articulated a common position on these issues. They called for a more representative international financial system. They sought greater voice for emerging economies in the
International Monetary Fund (IMF)
and
World Bank
. They also opposed protectionism and supported an open, rules-based multilateral trading system. This coordination laid the foundation for the
first BRIC Summit in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in 2009
.
BRIC was formally established in 2006
as a political cooperation forum among Brazil, Russia, India and China. Its founding members shared an aspiration for a more representative and equitable global order.
South Africa joined as a full member in 2011
, transforming
BRIC into BRICS.
This inclusion expanded the grouping’s geographical representation across continents.
The grouping subsequently broadened its agenda beyond economic issues to development, finance, health, climate action, technology and trade.
This evolution strengthened BRICS as a wider framework for engagement among emerging economies.
A Wider BRICS: Expanding Reach, Deepening Engagement
A major phase of expansion began in
January 2024
.
Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE
became full members.
Indonesia joined as the eleventh full member in January 2025.
These accessions significantly expanded BRICS’ geographical and economic reach. The expansion was accompanied by the creation of a
Partner Country category
.
Ten countries joined this framework during 2025:
Belarus, Bolivia, Cuba, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam. The new arrangement provides an additional channel for structured engagement with BRICS.
The Partner Country framework broadens BRICS’ outreach without altering its full-membership structure. It strengthens opportunities for
South-South cooperation
across Asia, Africa, Latin America and Eurasia. The wider network also creates scope for collaboration on trade, finance, climate action and sustainable development.
It reflects growing interest among emerging economies in participating in discussions on global governance.
The evolution of BRICS demonstrates a shift from a
four-country economic dialogue to a broader framework for political, economic, financial and social cooperation
. Its expansion has increased its demographic and economic weight. It has also broadened its regional representation and areas of engagement.
The grouping’s institutional evolution has kept pace with the changing priorities of emerging economies.
BRICS Presidency: Rotation and Responsibilities
The BRICS Presidency rotates annually according to the letters of its acronym. Each Presidency term begins on January 1st and concludes on December 31st of the respective year. The country holding the Presidency sets the priorities of the agenda for that year. It also organizes the group's annual Summit and steers key ministerial and working group meetings. With the recent expansion of BRICS membership, a new rotation formula for the Presidency is also being discussed among member countries.
India at the Helm of BRICS: From Continuity to Consensus
Before this year, India has previously chaired BRICS in
2012, 2016 and 2021
. Each Chairship reflected the priorities and challenges of its respective period. India’s repeated leadership demonstrates its sustained engagement with the grouping.
It also reflects India’s commitment to constructive multilateralism and the priorities of developing economies.
2012: Laying the Foundation for Stronger Cooperation
India hosted the
Fourth BRICS Summit
in New Delhi on
29 March 2012
. The Summit was held under the theme
“BRICS Partnership for Global Stability, Security and Prosperity.”
Discussions focused on global governance reform, sustainable development, food security and energy security. The Summit adopted the
Delhi Declaration
and an
Action Plan for strengthening BRICS cooperation
. The outcomes established a stronger foundation for institutional and sectoral engagement.
Click to Read More About the Delhi Declaration
Major Outcomes
The Summit proposed exploring a new Development Bank to mobilise resources for infrastructure and sustainable development projects. The proposed institution would serve BRICS, emerging economies and developing countries. It would complement existing multilateral and regional financial institutions in supporting global growth and development.
Click to Read More About the NDB.
Member nations signed the
Master Agreement on Extending Credit Facility in Local Currency
and boost intra-BRICS trade.
The summit also laid the foundation for the
Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA)
as a financial safety mechanism for BRICS countries. The arrangement was designed to provide short-term liquidity support and help member countries address financial instability.
India institutionalized new joint tracks for practical cooperation in agriculture, health, and science.
2016: Goa Summit Expanded BRICS Outreach
India hosted the
Eighth BRICS Summit
in Goa in October 2016. The Summit was held under the theme
“Building Responsive, Inclusive and Collective Solutions.”
India’s Chairship focused on strengthening intra-BRICS cooperation and expanding outreach. It also advanced collaboration on
counter-terrorism, trade, innovation and multilateral coordination
. The Goa Summit reinforced the grouping’s focus on emerging global challenges and practical cooperation.
Major Outcome
The operationalization of the New Development Bank was solidified with the rollout of its first set of financial loans, primarily backing renewable energy projects.
BRICS elevated
renewable energy access, clean energy transition and energy security
as shared priorities.
Greater focus was placed on combating
HIV and tuberculosis
.
India secured stronger BRICS language on combating terrorism and called for adherence to
FATF (
Financial Action Task Force
) standards
.
The
Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC)
Outreach Summit expanded engagement between BRICS and countries of the wider Bay of Bengal region. Discussions covered
counter-terrorism, trade, energy, investment, environment, technology and infrastructure
.
Agreement to establish
BRICS Agriculture Research Platform, BRICS Railway Research Network
,
BRICS Sports Council
and various youth-centric cooperation forums.
2021: Consolidating Cooperation in a Changing World
India hosted the
13th BRICS Summit virtually on 9 September 2021
. The Summit marked the
15th anniversary of BRICS
. It was held under the theme
“BRICS@15: Intra-BRICS Cooperation for Continuity, Consolidation and Consensus.”
India focused on strengthening institutional continuity, deepening cooperation and building greater consensus. The Chairship also advanced cooperation across health, digital technologies, counter-terrorism and sustainable development.
Major Outcomes
India led the adoption of a
unified BRICS Counter-Terrorism Action Plan.
Click to Read More about Action Plan.
India hosted the
first-ever BRICS Digital Health Summit
during its Chairship.
A BRICS Vaccine Research and Development Center was launched to collectively address current and future pandemic responses.
Agreement on Cooperation for the
BRICS Remote Sensing Satellite Constellation
. it enables countries to share remote-sensing data for environmental protection, disaster management, and climate monitoring.
India introduced new ministerial-level working paths, launching the
BRICS Alliance for Green Tourism
and the first
BRICS Water Ministers Meeting
for sustainable resource management.
Through successive Chairships, India has contributed to the institutional and substantive development of BRICS.
Its priorities have evolved with emerging global challenges while retaining a focus on practical cooperation.
India’s 2026 Chairship builds on this experience and the grouping’s expanded membership.
BRICS 2026: Key Outcomes Emerging from Ministerial Meetings
India assumed its
fourth BRICS Chairship
on 1 January 2026. During its Chairship, India convened a series of ministerial meetings across priority areas of BRICS cooperation. Over the year, BRICS members countries exchanged views on shared priorities and global and regional developments. These discussions advanced cooperation across the grouping’s three fundamental pillars. The pillars comprise
political and security cooperation, economic and financial cooperation, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges
.
More than
350 meetings and high-level engagements
were held across
25 cities
during India’s Chairship. The meetings generated
practical and development-oriented outcomes
across key areas of cooperation. The following outcomes emerged from
ministerial meetings held during India’s 2026 BRICS Chairship
.
BRICS Centres of Excellence on Agro-Ecology
agreed upon as a collaborative platform for joint research, knowledge sharing and capacity building on natural, organic and regenerative farming practices to promote climate-resilient and sustainable agricultural systems (initially coordinated by ICAR-Indian Institute of Farming Systems Research, Modipuram).
BRICS Network on Digital Agriculture
to deepen cooperation and scale the deployment of AI‑driven decision‑support systems, geospatial intelligence, IoT‑enabled monitoring, and advanced data analytics in agriculture (initially coordinated by IIT Delhi).
BRICS AGRIN (Agro-Inputs, Genetic Resources and Information Network)
agreed upon as a voluntary, farmer-centric cooperation framework among BRICS countries to strengthen collaboration in seeds, germplasm, and agricultural inputs.
BRICS Mission for Healthy Lifestyle
: The priority was launched along with the
BRICS Roadmap for a Joint Initiative on Healthy Lifestyle Promotion (2026-2029)
. It aims to serve as a collaborative platform for technical cooperation, knowledge exchange and coordinated awareness initiatives, promoting preventive and life-course approaches to obesity and other non-communicable diseases.
BRICS Expert Working Group on Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCIM)
: It aims to serve as a platform for structured and consensus-based cooperation on TCIM, covering policy dialogue, research and evidence generation, capacity building and academic exchange, digital knowledge platforms, quality and regulatory standards, and the protection of traditional and indigenous knowledge.
Focus on Mental Health
through
BRICS Training Hub Network
and
BRICS Network of Centres of Excellence
, with NIMHANS India as the coordinating Centre. It aims to optimize human resources for mental health through upskilling, task-sharing and standardized training, and to integrate mental well-being into primary healthcare.
Mainstreaming Traditional Knowledge
through adoption of
BRICS Principles for Advancing Climate Resilience through People-centric and Community-based Adaptation
and
BRICS Guiding Principles on Strengthening Academic Collaboration on Traditional and Indigenous Knowledge Systems
.
Advancing
Sustainable Lifestyles
through
Network of BRICS Institutions to Advance Knowledge Sharing, Research & Innovation
and
Sustainable Lifestyles Week
for exchange of knowledge on policies, programmes, initiatives and leading practices; conduct capacity-building workshops on thematic areas; facilitate dialogue among stakeholders including academic and research institutions; and compilation of case studies
.
BRICS CONNECT for Skilling
: A BRICS Cooperation Network for Capacity Building, Employability, and New Skills and Technologies (BRICS CONNECT), building on the BRICS Virtual Liaison Office. It is a flexible platform with four components, namely capacity building for advancing social security, women’s participation in the workforce, skills and employability, and digital public infrastructure. Cooperation under it is voluntary and non-binding.
Smart Grids and Energy Storage:
The
BRICS Guiding Principles on Energy Storage and Smart Grids
were adopted and the
BRICS Digital Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids and Energy Storage
was launched to serve as a voluntary platform for knowledge sharing, capacity building, the exchange of policy and regulatory best practices, and promotion of pilot initiatives among BRICS countries.
Urban Infrastructure strengthened
through establishment of
BRICS Urban Mobility Hub
, a virtual collaborative platform which will promote knowledge sharing, capacity building and technical cooperation in sustainable urban mobility; adoption of
BRICS Voluntary Principles for Climate Resilient Urban Infrastructure
to support the integration of climate and disaster risk considerations into urban planning, design, investment, construction, and maintenance; and establishment of a
BRICS Urban Research and Knowledge Network
for applied urban research, cross-border peer learning, and sustained institutional collaboration.
BRICS MSME Cooperation Portal,
to serve as a digital ecosystem accessible to all BRICS member countries, supporting MSMEs, technology centers and clusters, trade associations, financial institutions, training and capacity-building institutions, policymakers, and other relevant stakeholders, along with an institutionalized
Dialogue on MSME Finance
and
Workplan on the Internationalisation of MSMEs
were key outcomes to leverage BRICS for enhancing MSMEs’ access to markets and finance.
BRICS Incubator Network,
a digital interface/network to connect National Nodal Agencies, selected incubators and start-ups across BRICS countries, facilitate registration and linkages with participating incubators, and enable referral of qualified start-ups to incubators in other BRICS countries.
BRICS Startup Innovation Fund
to catalyse financing for early and growth stage startups and foster innovation driven entrepreneurship in BRICS countries.
BRICS Science and Research Repository
welcomed as a structured platform for scientific knowledge storage and sharing among BRICS countries.
BRICS Logistics Supply-Chain Cooperation Framework
: A voluntary, consensus-based framework to strengthen cross-sector transport logistics resilience and sustainability. It aims to address fragmented supply chains and weak connectivity by promoting technical exchange, knowledge sharing on cargo and shipping services, localized assembly and manufacturing ecosystems, and capacity building, while advancing environmentally sustainable and climate-resilient logistics practices.
BRICS Cooperation on Global Value Chains
through
GVC Action Plan 2026-2030,
including a Technical Council and GVC Joint Study for enhanced BRICS cooperation to ensure that GVCs are resilient, efficient and productive; and to advance the opening of markets and economic diversification among BRICS Members
.
BRICS Agreement on Cooperation and Mutual Administrative Assistance in Customs Matters:
Members confirmed their in-principle approval and willingness to sign the Agreement to support faster trade, lower transaction costs, more secure borders, trusted trade facilitation, improved ease of doing business, and tackling illicit trade.
Cooperation in the Field of Standardization
through an MoU signed by BRICS National Standards Body Heads, a formal framework to strengthen collaboration in the development, adoption and implementation of standards, promote information sharing, exchange of best practices, technical cooperation and capacity building, reinforce quality infrastructure, enhance consumer protection, reduce technical barriers to trade.
BRICS Youth Cooperation Framework 2026
adopted as a reference document to support continuity, coherence and structured cooperation to guide future dialogue, experience sharing and the consideration of practical initiatives under the BRICS Youth Track.
Sport Technology Cooperation institutionalized
through a new Working Group to promote cooperation in the field of sport technology in the form of exchange of good practices, institutional experiences, technical information and research inputs.
The ministerial meeting outcomes under India’s 2026 BRICS Chairship reflect a continued focus on practical cooperation, inclusive growth and a stronger voice for the Global South.
2026:
Steering BRICS Towards a More Inclusive Future
India’s
2026 BRICS Chairship
comes at a time of significant global transformation. The international system is experiencing economic fragmentation, technological disruption and geopolitical uncertainty. Climate change and resource pressures are adding further complexity.
These interconnected challenges require cooperation that is inclusive, practical and responsive to diverse national circumstances.
BRICS provides an important avenue for addressing these challenges through dialogue and coordinated action. Its expanded membership brings diverse perspectives from major emerging economies.
The grouping can help advance cooperation on development, climate action, technology, energy and financial resilience.
It can also contribute to discussions on reforms in global institutions.
For India, the objective extends beyond expanding the grouping’s scale.
It is about converting greater representation into meaningful cooperation and tangible outcomes.
India’s Chairship seeks to build consensus across diverse members while strengthening the effectiveness of existing mechanisms.
India aims to reinforce BRICS as a constructive force for a more inclusive global order.
